title: HIS-201 Ch. 5 — 4 Main Ideas
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 5: The Mosaic of Eighteenth-Century America

cards.def: Fearing that French and Russian rivals would threaten New Spain, Spain pushed missions and presidios into Texas and California, but they stayed thin outposts surrounded by powerful Indians like the Comanches.
France had the same problem of too few colonists, so New France relied on compromise and alliances with Indians, while slave-based Louisiana struggled after the 1729 Natchez uprising.

British colonies instead boomed through natural increase, immigration and slave imports, but newcomers, backcountry settlement and growing seaports split colonists by ethnicity, region, class and religion.
Massive imports of Africans made the South more embattled, as enslaved people slowly built families and an African American culture and resisted through sabotage, escape and the 1739 Stono Rebellion.

Religion divided colonists further, as Enlightenment reason bred rational Christianity among a few, while the Great Awakening's emotional call for a "new birth" split churches and spread Presbyterians and Baptists.

Despite these divisions, most white colonists took pride in being English, because Britain's benign neglect gave them greater economic opportunity, wider landownership and more representative governments than England had.
